pos: v. (to declare righteous; rendering Hebrew tsadaq, Greek dikaioo)
etymology: From Latin justificare, to make or declare just. The word is forensic before it is moral: a verdict pronounced, not a quality infused.
biblical_def: To justify is to declare a person righteous in law. The Reformed reading turns on the courtroom sense, and Scripture insists on it: God “justifieth the ungodly” (Rom 4:5), which would be monstrous if justify meant to make good — a judge who made a wicked man good would be a reformer, not a judge; a judge who declares the ungodly righteous must have a ground outside the man. That ground is Christ: “being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 3:24). The proof that the word is declarative is that Scripture forbids the opposite verdict in the same breath — he that justifieth the wicked is abomination (Pro 17:15) — unless a ransom has satisfied the law.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines justify as to prove or show to be just, to vindicate, and in theology to pardon and clear from guilt — to treat as righteous.
webster_full: JUSTIFY, v.t. To prove or show to be just, or conformable to law, right, justice, propriety or duty; to defend or maintain; to vindicate as right.
2. In theology, to pardon and clear from guilt; to absolve or acquit from guilt and merited punishment, and to accept as righteous on account of the merits of the Savior.
scriptures: Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Rom 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.
Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Justification has been quietly reworded from a verdict into a process — God helping a man become acceptable — which removes assurance at the root, since a process is never finished.
corruption_paragraphs: The pastoral cost of turning the verdict into a process is exact and measurable: assurance dies. If justification is God declaring me righteous on Christ's account, the verdict is as settled as the cross that grounds it, and Romans 5:1 follows — therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God. If justification is God gradually making me righteous, then peace waits on progress, and no honest man ever has enough.

The counterfeit runs the other direction too, in a lawlessness that treats the verdict as indifference. But the God who justifies the ungodly does not wink; He is just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus (Rom 3:26). The verdict costs blood. Grace that cost nothing was never this doctrine.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsadaq (H6663), to be right, to declare right; Greek dikaioo (G1344), to pronounce righteous — the verb of the lawcourt, not the workshop.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsadaq (H6663) — to be just, to declare righteous; Isaiah 53:11, by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many.
Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, acquit; Romans 3:24, 4:5, 5:1, Galatians 2:16.
Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness; the standing conferred by the verdict.
usage: “Him that justifieth the ungodly” — the verdict must rest on a ground outside the man.
“He that justifieth the wicked… is abomination” — which is why the cross was necessary.
“Being justified by faith, we have peace with God” — a settled verdict yields settled peace.

pos: v. (to restore to friendship; rendering Greek katallasso)
etymology: From Latin reconciliare, to bring together again. The Bible's reconciliation is never mutual negotiation; the offended party initiates and bears the cost.
biblical_def: To reconcile is to end enmity and restore fellowship. Scripture's grammar is startling: it is always God who reconciles and man who is reconciled — “all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ” (2Co 5:18). The offended Judge does not wait to be appeased by the offender; He provides the appeasement Himself and then sends ambassadors to beg the guilty to accept it. Paul dates it precisely: “when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Rom 5:10). Christ makes the horizontal follow the vertical, ordering a man to leave his gift at the altar and be reconciled to his brother first (Mat 5:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reconcile as to conciliate anew, to call back into union and friendship the affections which have been alienated; to restore to favor.
webster_full: RECONCILE, v.t. To conciliate anew; to call back into union and friendship the affections which have been alienated; to restore to friendship or favor after estrangement.
2. To bring to acquiescence, content or quiet submission.
3. To make consistent or congruous; to bring to agreement.
scriptures: And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation;
Rom 5:10
For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.
Mat 5:24
Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.
Col 1:21
And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled
corruption_summary: Reconciliation is preached as mutual meeting in the middle — both sides conceding — which flatters the guilty party and empties the cross of its necessity.
corruption_paragraphs: Between God and man there is no middle. The enmity is not a misunderstanding to be talked through but a moral breach in which one party is entirely in the wrong, and the reconciliation is therefore one-directional: God reconciles, at His own cost, on His own terms. Colossians states the before plainly — you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled (Col 1:21). Any preaching that lets a sinner arrive at the table as a negotiating equal has not read the terms.

The horizontal application is where the church actually fails. Christ's command interrupts worship itself — leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother — which means a congregation full of unreconciled members is offering gifts God has told them to set down. Reconciliation among brethren is not optional emotional hygiene; it is a precondition of acceptable worship.
roots_summary: Greek katallasso (G2644), to exchange, to change enmity for friendship; the noun katallage (G2643) is the ministry Paul was given.
roots_lines: Greek katallasso (G2644) — to reconcile; Romans 5:10, 2 Corinthians 5:18-20.
Greek katallage (G2643) — reconciliation, the atonement of Romans 5:11.
Greek apokatallasso (G604) — to reconcile completely; Colossians 1:20-21, Ephesians 2:16.
usage: “God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ” — the offended party initiates.
“When we were enemies, we were reconciled” — the timing rules out our contribution.
“First be reconciled to thy brother” — worship waits on the horizontal.

pos: v. (to reckon to one's account; rendering Hebrew chashab, Greek logizomai)
etymology: From Latin imputare, to enter in the reckoning — a bookkeeping word. Scripture's most consequential accounting entries are made with it.
biblical_def: To impute is to credit or charge something to an account. Three imputations carry the whole gospel: Adam's sin reckoned to his race, our sin reckoned to Christ, and Christ's righteousness reckoned to us. The pivotal text is Abraham's: “he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness” (Gen 15:6), which Paul presses into a doctrine — “to him that worketh not, but believeth… his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5). The blessedness of the man is stated as a negative entry: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin” (Rom 4:8). Nothing is transferred by infusion; everything is transferred by reckoning.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impute as to charge, to attribute, to set to the account of — and specifically, in theology, to attribute vicariously.
webster_full: IMPUTE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of; generally ill, sometimes good.
2. To attribute; to ascribe.
3. In theology, to impute is to charge or attribute vicariously; as, the righteousness of Christ is imputed to believers.
scriptures: Gen 15:6
And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Rom 4:8
Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
corruption_summary: Imputation is dismissed as a legal fiction, as though God pretended — when in fact it is the only category that lets a holy God receive sinners without lying about them.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge of legal fiction misunderstands what a reckoning is. When a debt is paid by another and the ledger is marked settled, nothing false has been recorded; the account genuinely stands clear because the payment genuinely occurred. 2 Corinthians 5:21 states the double entry with precision: he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Christ was not made sinful, nor are we made intrinsically righteous — the reckoning is real because the substitution was real.

Where the doctrine is lost, sanctification is immediately corrupted, because the believer starts trying to establish the standing he has already been given. Imputed righteousness is the ground a Christian stands on while he is being made holy; delete it and holiness becomes the anxious manufacture of a standing, which Scripture calls going about to establish their own righteousness (Rom 10:3).
roots_summary: Hebrew chashab (H2803), to reckon, to account; Greek logizomai (G3049), to count up, put to one's account — used eleven times in Romans 4 alone.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, impute; Genesis 15:6, counted to him for righteousness.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, credit; Romans 4:3-11, 2 Corinthians 5:19, not imputing their trespasses.
Greek ellogeo (G1677) — to charge to an account; Philemon 18, put that on mine account.
usage: “He counted it to him for righteousness” — the entry that founds the doctrine.
“Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin” — blessedness as an accounting negative.
“Put that on mine account” — Paul enacts imputation for a runaway slave.

pos: n. (forgiveness, release; rendering Greek aphesis)
etymology: From Latin remittere, to send back or release. A remitted debt is not reduced but sent away.
biblical_def: Remission is the release of guilt and its penalty. Hebrews states the price and the rule in one line: “without shedding of blood is no remission” (Heb 9:22) — forgiveness in Scripture is never free-floating clemency but always purchased release. Christ names His blood as the purchase: “this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Mat 26:28). Peter makes it the terms of the first gospel sermon: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins” (Act 2:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines remission as forgiveness, pardon, the giving up of the punishment due to a crime; release from a debt or claim.
webster_full: REMISSION, n. Forgiveness; pardon; that is, the giving up of the punishment due to a crime.
2. The act of sending back.
3. Release; discharge or relinquishment of a claim or right; as the remission of a debt.
scriptures: Heb 9:22
And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.
For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.
Act 2:38
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: Forgiveness is now assumed as God's default temperament rather than purchased release — a costless remission that quietly makes Calvary unnecessary.
corruption_paragraphs: If God forgives simply because forgiving is the sort of thing He does, the cross becomes an extravagant redundancy and Hebrews 9:22 an embarrassment. The whole sacrificial system exists to teach the opposite instinct: guilt is real, it must be borne by someone, and blood marks the bearing. Remission is glorious precisely because it was not free — it was free to us and ruinous to Him.

The second corruption is to leave remission unpreached to the actual guilty. Christ's commission specifies the content: that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations (Luk 24:47). A pulpit that offers meaning, purpose, and belonging but never announces the release of guilt has changed the subject of the gospel.
roots_summary: Greek aphesis (G859), a sending away, release — the same word for the release of prisoners and of debts; from aphiemi, to let go.
roots_lines: Greek aphesis (G859) — release, forgiveness; Matthew 26:28, Acts 2:38, Ephesians 1:7.
Greek aphiemi (G863) — to send away, forgive; the verb of the Lord's Prayer, forgive us our debts.
Hebrew nasa (H5375) — to lift, bear away; the Old Testament picture of guilt carried off, as by the scapegoat.
usage: “Without shedding of blood is no remission” — the rule that makes the cross necessary.
“My blood… shed for many for the remission of sins” — the purchase named at the table.
“Repentance and remission of sins should be preached” — the commission's content.

pos: v. (to step across a boundary; rendering Hebrew abar and pasha)
etymology: From Latin transgredi, to step across. Sin under this word is not weakness but trespass — a line known and crossed.
biblical_def: To transgress is to cross a boundary God has set. The word presupposes a published law, which is why it is the sharpest of the sin-words: “Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?” (Mat 15:3). Israel's covenant history is summarized by it — “they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant” (Isa 24:5). And the danger of transgressing runs in both directions: Christ charges the Pharisees with crossing God's line to keep their own, showing that religious scrupulosity is no protection against trespass.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines transgress as to pass over or beyond any limit; to violate a law, civil or moral; to offend by violating a law.
webster_full: TRANSGRESS, v.t. To pass over or beyond any limit.
2. To overpass any rule prescribed as the limit of duty; to break or violate a law, civil or moral.
TRANSGRESS, v.i. To offend by violating a law; to sin.
scriptures: Mat 15:3
But he answered and said unto them, Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?
Isa 24:5
The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant.
Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee.
Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law.
corruption_summary: An age with no fixed boundaries cannot transgress — only underperform — so sin is rebranded as brokenness, and the one word that implies a Lawgiver quietly disappears.
corruption_paragraphs: Every synonym the modern church prefers — brokenness, woundedness, unhealthy patterns — describes a condition rather than an act against a Person. Transgression insists on the Person: there is a line, He drew it, and I crossed it knowing. That is worse news and better news at once, because a condition can only be managed while a trespass can be forgiven.

Christ's use in Matthew 15 catches the religious version. The Pharisees were not libertines; they were boundary-keepers who had erected their own fence and stepped over God's to maintain it. Any tradition — including a conservative one — that requires disobeying a plain command in order to be observed has become the very transgression it was built to prevent.
roots_summary: Hebrew abar (H5674), to pass over; pasha (H6586), to rebel or break away; Greek parabaino (G3845), to step beside or across.
roots_lines: Hebrew abar (H5674) — to cross over; the same verb for crossing Jordan and for crossing God's command.
Hebrew pasha (H6586) — to rebel, transgress; the word behind transgressors in Isaiah 53:12.
Greek parabaino (G3845) — to overstep; Matthew 15:3, and the noun parabasis in Romans 4:15.
usage: “Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?” — religious fences can cause the trespass.
“They have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance” — the covenant indictment.
“Then will I teach transgressors thy ways” — the forgiven man's vocation.

pos: v. (to cause to stumble; rendering Greek skandalizo)
etymology: From Latin offendere, to strike against. The Greek behind it names the trigger-stick of a trap — to offend is to set a snare in a brother's path.
biblical_def: To offend in Scripture is rarely to hurt feelings; it is to cause someone to stumble into sin. Christ's severity is proportioned to that meaning: “whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck” (Mat 18:6). The remedy He prescribes is directed at oneself first — “if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out” (Mat 5:29) — and Paul takes the principle into Christian liberty, resolving to eat no flesh while the world stands rather than make his brother to offend (1Co 8:13). Meanwhile Christ Himself is a rock of offence to the proud, and that stumbling is not to be removed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines offend as to attack, to assail; to displease, to make angry; and to cause to stumble or to sin.
webster_full: OFFEND, v.t. To attack; to assail. [Not used.]
2. To displease; to make angry; to affront.
3. To be scandalous to; to cause to stumble; to cause to sin or neglect duty.
scriptures: Mat 18:6
But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.
Mat 5:29
And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend.
Rom 9:33
As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.
corruption_summary: The word has collapsed into taking offence — a matter of injured sensitivity — so that the only offending anyone fears is rudeness, while causing a brother to stumble goes unnamed.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors follow the collapse. The first sacrifices truth to avoid giving offence in the modern sense, and calls the sacrifice love; but the gospel contains a stone of stumbling laid by God Himself (Rom 9:33), and no preacher has authority to remove it. The second grows careless about the biblical sense, exercising liberty without a glance at the weaker brother — and Paul's standard there is extreme: he would abandon a lawful thing permanently rather than trip a saint.

Christ's self-directed remedy is the part almost never quoted. If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out. Before a disciple audits what others do to him, he is told to amputate whatever in his own life functions as a trap. An offence-conscious church that never applies the knife inward has inverted the sermon.
roots_summary: Greek skandalizo (G4624), to put a stumbling-block in the way; from skandalon (G4625), the bait-stick of a trap.
roots_lines: Greek skandalizo (G4624) — to cause to stumble; Matthew 5:29, 18:6, 1 Corinthians 8:13.
Greek skandalon (G4625) — a trap-stick, snare; the rock of offence in Romans 9:33.
Greek proskomma (G4348) — a stumbling; Romans 14:13, that no man put a stumblingblock in his brother's way.
usage: “Whoso shall offend one of these little ones… a millstone” — the severity fits the real meaning.
“If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out” — the first audit is inward.
“I will eat no flesh while the world standeth” — liberty surrendered for a brother.

pos: n. (craft, deceit; rendering Hebrew mirmah, Greek dolos)
etymology: From Old French guile, deceit — a cousin of wile. The Greek dolos originally meant bait for a hook, which is exactly how guile works.
biblical_def: Guile is deceit that baits. Scripture uses its absence as the highest compliment: Christ says of Nathanael, “Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile” (Joh 1:47) — a pointed contrast with Jacob, the father of the nation, who got the birthright by guile. The blessed man of Psalm 32 is defined by the same absence: “Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile” (Psa 32:2). Of the Servant it is said, “neither was any deceit in his mouth” (Isa 53:9), and Peter makes that the pattern for the flock (1Pe 2:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines guile as craft, cunning, artifice, duplicity — usually in a bad sense; deceitful cunning.
webster_full: GUILE, n. Craft; cunning; artifice; duplicity; deceit; usually in a bad sense.
GUILE, v.t. To disguise craftily. [Not used.]
scriptures: Joh 1:47
Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!
Psa 32:2
Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile.
Isa 53:9
And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth:
corruption_summary: Guile has been professionalized — renamed strategy, positioning, and personal branding — so that the baited hook is now a skill set rather than a sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 32 places guilelessness inside the doctrine of forgiveness, and the order repays attention: the man whose iniquity is not imputed is the man in whose spirit there is no guile. The connection is not that honesty earns pardon, but that a pardoned man no longer needs to manage his image. Guile is the labor of a soul defending a reputation it cannot afford to lose; imputed righteousness makes that labor unnecessary and therefore ridiculous.

The church's version is guile in the service of good ends — inflated numbers, curated testimonies, the ministry brand. Paul explicitly renounced it: not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully (2Co 4:2). A gospel about a Man in whose mouth was no deceit cannot be advanced by a bait-and-switch, however successful.
roots_summary: Hebrew mirmah (H4820), deceit, treachery; Greek dolos (G1388), bait, craft — the word for a hook's lure.
roots_lines: Hebrew mirmah (H4820) — deceit; used of Jacob's taking of the blessing with subtilty (Gen 27:35).
Greek dolos (G1388) — bait, guile; John 1:47, 1 Peter 2:1 and 2:22.
Greek adolos (G97) — without guile; the sincere milk of the word, 1 Peter 2:2.
usage: “An Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile” — the compliment that indicts Jacob.
“In whose spirit there is no guile” — the forgiven need no image management.
“Neither was any deceit in his mouth” — the Servant's silence under injustice.

pos: n. (what is owed; rendering Hebrew chob, Greek opheilema)
etymology: From Latin debitum, that which is owed. Christ chose the word for the model prayer, making sin an obligation rather than a mere stain.
biblical_def: A debt is something owed. Christ teaches His disciples to name sin this way — “forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Mat 6:12) — and then presses the metaphor to breaking point in the parable of the servant forgiven ten thousand talents who throttles a fellow servant over a hundred pence (Mat 18:32–33). Paul allows the believer exactly one standing debt: “Owe no man any thing, but to love one another” (Rom 13:8). The Old Testament surrounds debt with mercy legislation, since the borrower is servant to the lender (Pro 22:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines debt as that which is due from one person to another, whether money, goods or services; and that which one is bound to pay or perform.
webster_full: DEBT, n. That which is due from one person to another, whether money, goods or services; that which one person is bound to pay or perform to another.
2. That which any one is obliged to do or to suffer.
3. In scripture, sin; trespass; guilt; crime.
scriptures: Mat 6:12
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
Then his lord, after that he had called him, said unto him, O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me:
Rom 13:8
Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.
Pro 22:7
The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
corruption_summary: A civilization built on permanent debt has lost the ability to hear sin described as debt — and a church casual about borrowing cannot preach the parable it lives inside.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the unmerciful servant depends on a ratio: ten thousand talents against a hundred pence, a debt beyond any lifetime's earning set beside a trivial sum. The unforgiving Christian has not miscalculated his brother's offence; he has miscalculated his own. Where sin is felt as a manageable shortfall rather than an unpayable debt, forgiveness of others becomes optional, and the parable ends where Christ ends it — with the servant delivered to the tormentors.

Proverbs 22:7 is not a curse but a description: the borrower is servant to the lender. Scripture nowhere forbids borrowing outright, but it never treats debt as neutral, and it hedges lending with sabbath-year release, prohibitions on usury against a brother, and the return of a poor man's pledge before nightfall. A church that ignores all of that while urging its members toward whatever the culture finances has surrendered a genuine field of discipleship.
roots_summary: Hebrew chob (H2326), debt; Greek opheilema (G3783), what is owed — the word in the Lord's Prayer; daneion (G1156) is the loan of the parable.
roots_lines: Greek opheilema (G3783) — a debt, that which is owed; Matthew 6:12, and Romans 4:4 of wages reckoned as debt not grace.
Greek opheiletes (G3781) — a debtor; Matthew 6:12, Romans 1:14, I am debtor both to the Greeks and to the Barbarians.
Hebrew nashah (H5383) — to lend on interest; the root behind Israel's usury laws.
usage: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” — sin named as obligation.
“Owe no man any thing, but to love one another” — the one debt left standing.
“The borrower is servant to the lender” — a description, not a curse.

pos: n. (one who owes; rendering Greek opheiletes)
etymology: From debt, Latin debitor. Paul takes the commercial word and makes it the posture of a missionary.
biblical_def: A debtor is one under obligation. Scripture puts believers in the position twice over. First as forgiven sinners, taught to pray as those who have debtors of their own (Mat 6:12). Second, and more surprisingly, as those who owe the gospel to the world: “I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians; both to the wise, and to the unwise” (Rom 1:14). Paul had received nothing from Rome, yet he reckoned himself in their debt, because a trust received for others creates an obligation toward them. Christ's parable of the two debtors adds the affections: he to whom most is forgiven loves most (Luk 7:41–43).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines debtor as one who owes another, either money, goods or services; and one who is under obligation to another.
webster_full: DEBTOR, n. The person who owes another either money, goods or services.
2. One who is under obligation to another; as, we are all debtors to the divine goodness.
3. In book-keeping, the person or side of an account which receives value.
scriptures: Rom 1:14
I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians; both to the wise, and to the unwise.
Mat 6:12
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
Luk 7:41
There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty.
Luk 7:47
Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.
corruption_summary: Mission is now framed as generosity from the strong to the needy — a favour conferred — where Paul framed it as a debt owed, which produces a very different missionary.
corruption_paragraphs: The difference between a benefactor and a debtor shows up under pressure. A benefactor evangelizes while it is rewarding and stops when it is thankless, because a gift may be withdrawn. A debtor pays whether or not the creditor is grateful, because the obligation is not contingent on reception. Paul's I am debtor is therefore not humility-flavoured rhetoric; it is the engine that carried him to cities that stoned him.

Luke 7 supplies the affections that keep the debt from becoming grim. The woman who wept over Christ's feet was the larger debtor, and her love was proportioned to her forgiveness — to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little. Cold Christianity is nearly always the fruit of a small estimate of one's own account, not of a difficult temperament.
roots_summary: Greek opheiletes (G3781), one who owes; chreopheiletes (G5533), a debtor in the strict commercial sense, used in Luke's parables.
roots_lines: Greek opheiletes (G3781) — debtor; Matthew 6:12, Romans 1:14, Romans 8:12, we are debtors, not to the flesh.
Greek chreopheiletes (G5533) — a money-debtor; Luke 7:41 and 16:5.
Greek charizomai (G5483) — to forgive freely; the creditor's action in Luke 7:42, he frankly forgave them both.
usage: “I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians” — mission as obligation, not favour.
“He frankly forgave them both” — the creditor's freeness sets the love.
“To whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little” — cold love reveals a small estimate of the debt.

pos: adj., n. (rejected after testing; rendering Greek adokimos)
etymology: From Latin reprobare, to reject on trial — the opposite of approbare. The metal was assayed and failed; the word carries the smell of the refiner's fire.
biblical_def: Reprobate means rejected after examination. The Greek adokimos is a metallurgist's term for metal that failed the assay, and Scripture applies it three ways: to a mind God gives men over to when they refuse Him (Rom 1:28), to silver that the LORD has rejected (Jer 6:30), and — most searchingly — as a question every professing believer is told to put to himself: “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith… know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?” (2Co 13:5). Paul feared it for himself, disciplining his body lest he should be a castaway — the same word (1Co 9:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reprobate as not enduring proof or trial; abandoned in sin; lost to virtue or grace — and as a noun, one abandoned to error or apostasy.
webster_full: REPROBATE, a. Not enduring proof or trial; not of standard purity or fineness; disallowed; rejected.
2. Abandoned in sin; lost to virtue or grace.
REPROBATE, n. A person abandoned to sin; one lost to virtue and religion.
scriptures: Rom 1:28
And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient;
Jer 6:30
Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the LORD hath rejected them.
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
corruption_summary: The word is used almost exclusively as a label for other people, when the New Testament aims it at the mirror — examine yourselves.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 1:28 shows the mechanism, and it is judicial rather than arbitrary: because they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind. The rejection of God comes first; the rejected mind is the sentence. That order should terrify a culture that has spent decades cultivating the first half while treating the second as unthinkable.

But Paul will not let the doctrine stay pointed outward. He applies the assay to himself — lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway — and commands the Corinthians to test themselves rather than him. Self-examination is not morbid introspection; it is the ordinary discipline of people who believe the assay is real and would rather discover a failure now than at the judgment.
roots_summary: Greek adokimos (G96), failing the test, rejected; the negative of dokimos (G1384), approved after trial — both drawn from metal assaying.
roots_lines: Greek adokimos (G96) — unapproved, rejected; Romans 1:28, 2 Corinthians 13:5, Titus 1:16, 1 Corinthians 9:27.
Greek dokimos (G1384) — tested and approved; Romans 16:10, James 1:12, the crown for the man who is approved.
Hebrew maas (H3988) — to reject; Jeremiah 6:30, reprobate silver shall men call them.
usage: “God gave them over to a reprobate mind” — the sentence follows the refusal.
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith” — the assay aimed at the mirror.
“Lest… I myself should be a castaway” — the apostle applies it to himself.

pos: n. (a covenant, a will; rendering Greek diatheke)
etymology: From Latin testamentum, a will. The Greek diatheke carries both senses — covenant and last will — and Hebrews exploits the double meaning deliberately.
biblical_def: A testament is a covenant, and in one crucial passage a will. Christ names the cup with it: “this cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you” (Luk 22:20). Hebrews then presses the legal sense to prove the necessity of the death: “where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator” (Heb 9:16). A will confers an inheritance the heir did not earn and cannot negotiate, and it takes effect only when the one who made it dies. That is why the gospel is announced rather than negotiated: the terms were set by the Testator, and He has died.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines testament as a solemn authentic instrument in writing by which a person declares his will as to the disposal of his estate after death; and the name of each general division of the Scriptures.
webster_full: TESTAMENT, n. A solemn authentic instrument in writing, by which a person declares his will as to the disposal of his estate and effects after his death.
2. The name of each general division of the canonical books of the sacred Scriptures; as the Old Testament; the New Testament.
scriptures: Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.
Heb 9:16
For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator.
Heb 9:17
For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth.
Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
corruption_summary: Covenant language has been softened into partnership and relationship — warm words that carry no inheritance, no testator, and no death.
corruption_paragraphs: The genius of Hebrews 9 is that it will not let the reader keep the benefit while losing the blood. A testament confers real property, but only over the testator's corpse; therefore the new covenant's blessings — forgiveness, a written-on heart, God as our God — are not aspirations but bequests, legally settled by a death that has already occurred. Assurance rests on probate, not on the heir's performance.

Jeremiah 31 shows what is bequeathed, and it is deliberately unconditional in its verbs: I will put my law in their inward parts, I will be their God, I will forgive their iniquity. A partnership would require both parties to perform; a testament requires only that the Testator's will be executed. Losing this vocabulary is how congregations end up working to secure what they have already inherited.
roots_summary: Greek diatheke (G1242), a disposition, covenant, will — the Septuagint's word for the Hebrew berith, covenant.
roots_lines: Greek diatheke (G1242) — covenant, testament; Luke 22:20, Hebrews 9:15-17, Hebrews 8:8 quoting Jeremiah.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the cut agreement of Genesis 15 and Jeremiah 31:31.
Greek kleronomia (G2817) — inheritance; what a testament conveys, 1 Peter 1:4, incorruptible and undefiled.
usage: “This cup is the new testament in my blood” — the will read aloud at the table.
“There must also of necessity be the death of the testator” — why the cross was not optional.
“I will make a new covenant… I will forgive their iniquity” — bequests, not negotiations.

pos: n., v. (censure, fault; rendering Greek momos and amemptos in the negative)
etymology: From Old French blasmer, ultimately from Greek blasphemein, to speak evil of. Blame and blasphemy share a root: both are speech against.
biblical_def: Blame is censure justly or unjustly laid, and Scripture's interest is mostly in being without it. Election has a stated goal: “that we should be holy and without blame before him in love” (Eph 1:4). Paul defends his own conduct in handling money by an unusual standard — “avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us” (2Co 8:20) — taking pains not merely to be honest but to be visibly beyond suspicion. And when Peter was blameworthy, Paul withstood him to the face, “because he was to be blamed” (Gal 2:11): apostolic office was no shelter from correction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blame as to censure, to express disapprobation of, to find fault with; and as a noun, imputation of a fault, censure, or the fault itself.
webster_full: BLAME, v.t. To censure; to express disapprobation of; to find fault with; opposed to praise or commend.
2. To bring reproach upon; to blemish; to injure.
BLAME, n. Imputation of a fault; censure; reprehension.
scriptures: Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us:
Gal 2:11
But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
Php 2:15
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world;
corruption_summary: Two ditches: a therapeutic culture that treats all blame as abuse, and a religious culture that assigns it freely to everyone except its own leaders.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's money practice in 2 Corinthians 8 deserves to be church policy. He arranged for a brother chosen by the churches to travel with the collection, expressly so that no man should blame us — not because he was dishonest, but because handling other people's money without accountability invites suspicion that honesty alone cannot dispel. Ministries that resist audit while protesting their integrity have exactly reversed the apostolic instinct.

Galatians 2 settles the other question. Peter — the first among the apostles, an eyewitness of the resurrection — was blamed publicly by Paul for withdrawing from Gentile tables, because the gospel itself was at stake. Where a church has made its leaders structurally unblameable, it has not protected them; it has removed the mechanism by which Peter was kept from wrecking the doctrine of justification.
roots_summary: Greek amomos (G299), without spot or blemish; amemptos (G273), blameless; memphomai (G3201), to find fault — the vocabulary is largely negative by design.
roots_lines: Greek amomos (G299) — unblemished; Ephesians 1:4, and of the Lamb without blemish, 1 Peter 1:19.
Greek amemptos (G273) — blameless; Philippians 2:15, that ye may be blameless and harmless.
Greek kataginosko (G2607) — to be condemned, blamed; Galatians 2:11 of Peter at Antioch.
usage: “Holy and without blame before him in love” — election's stated goal.
“That no man should blame us in this abundance” — visible accountability with money.
“Because he was to be blamed” — no office is above correction.

pos: n. (a judicial decision; rendering Greek krima and apokrima)
etymology: From Latin sententia, an opinion or judgment pronounced. In Scripture the word belongs to the bench, not the grammar book.
biblical_def: A sentence is a judgment pronounced. Ecclesiastes diagnoses the danger of a slow one: “Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil” (Ecc 8:11). Paul describes his brush with death as having “the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead” (2Co 1:9). And at the Jerusalem council James renders one: “my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God” (Act 15:19) — a judgment that kept the gospel free.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sentence as a judgment pronounced by a court or judge upon a criminal; a determination or decision given.
webster_full: SENTENCE, n. In law, a judgment pronounced by a court or judge upon a person on trial for a crime or offense.
2. A determination or decision given, particularly on some disputed point.
3. A short saying containing moral instruction; a maxim.
scriptures: Ecc 8:11
Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead:
Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God:
Deu 17:9
And thou shalt come unto the priests the Levites, and unto the judge that shall be in those days, and enquire; and they shall shew thee the sentence of judgment:
corruption_summary: Delayed judgment is read as no judgment — exactly the error Ecclesiastes names — while a culture of endless appeal teaches that no sentence is ever final.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 8:11 is one of the most useful verses in Scripture for reading a civilization. The mechanism is not that men conclude God does not exist; it is that the gap between the deed and the sentence is long enough for the conscience to lose the connection, and so hearts become fully set to do evil. God's patience, designed for repentance, is misread as approval — which is why 2 Peter has to insist that the Lord is not slack concerning his promise.

Paul's use inverts the terror. He received the sentence of death in himself, and names its purpose: that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead. For the believer, the sentence has already fallen on a Substitute, so the experience of dying becomes an instrument of faith rather than a foretaste of wrath. Same word, opposite outcome, and the cross is the difference.
roots_summary: Greek krima (G2917), a judicial decision; apokrima (G610), a sentence passed; Hebrew pithgam (H6599), a decree, in Ecclesiastes 8:11.
roots_lines: Greek apokrima (G610) — a judicial sentence; only 2 Corinthians 1:9.
Greek krima (G2917) — judgment, condemnation; Romans 5:16, the judgment was by one to condemnation.
Hebrew pithgam (H6599) — decree, sentence; Ecclesiastes 8:11, Esther 1:20.
usage: “Sentence… is not executed speedily” — delay misread as acquittal.
“We had the sentence of death in ourselves” — a verdict that teaches faith.
“My sentence is, that we trouble not them” — the ruling that kept the gospel free.

pos: n. (a formal request; rendering Hebrew sheelah, Greek aitema)
etymology: From Latin petitio, a seeking or request. A petition is prayer with a specific ask in it — the opposite of vague religious sentiment.
biblical_def: A petition is a definite request. John grounds Christian confidence on it: “if we know that he hear us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him” (1Jn 5:15). Hannah's vow at Shiloh is answered in the same vocabulary — “the LORD grant thee thy petition that thou hast asked of him” (1Sa 1:17) — and the word carries the danger too, since Daniel's enemies engineered a law against asking any petition of any God save the king, which sent him to the lions rather than to silence (Dan 6:7–10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines petition as a request, supplication or prayer; a solemn or formal supplication, particularly to a superior or to the Supreme Being.
webster_full: PETITION, n. In a general sense, a request, supplication or prayer; but chiefly and appropriately, a solemn or formal supplication.
2. A formal request or supplication, verbal or written; particularly, a written supplication from an inferior to a superior.
3. The paper containing a supplication.
scriptures: And if we know that he hear us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him.
Then Eli answered and said, Go in peace: and the God of Israel grant thee thy petition that thou hast asked of him.
Dan 6:7

All the presidents of the kingdom, the governors, and the princes, the counsellors, and the captains, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree, that whosoever shall ask a petition of any God or man for thirty days, save of thee, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.
Php 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
corruption_summary: Petition has been talked out of prayer as immature — real prayer being contemplation or alignment — when Scripture's model prayers are almost entirely made of specific asks.
corruption_paragraphs: The prayer Christ taught is six petitions long and unembarrassed about it: hallowed, come, be done, give, forgive, deliver. Philippians 4:6 doubles down — in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. The mature-sounding preference for wordless alignment over definite asking would have edited the Lord's Prayer down to nothing, and it quietly removes the very thing that makes answered prayer recognizable.

Daniel 6 shows what petitioning costs when a state decides who may be asked. The decree did not forbid believing in God; it forbade petitioning Him. Daniel's response was not to petition more quietly but to keep his windows open toward Jerusalem three times a day as he did aforetime — the unremarkable habit becoming the point of resistance.
roots_summary: Hebrew sheelah (H7596), a request asked; Greek aitema (G155), a thing requested; deesis (G1162), supplication arising from need.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheelah (H7596) — petition, request; 1 Samuel 1:17 and 1:27, for this child I prayed.
Greek aitema (G155) — a request; 1 John 5:15, Philippians 4:6.
Greek deesis (G1162) — supplication from need; the effectual fervent prayer of James 5:16.
usage: “We have the petitions that we desired of him” — confidence attaches to definite asks.
“The LORD grant thee thy petition” — Eli's word over Hannah.
“Let your requests be made known unto God” — anxiety's prescribed alternative.

pos: n. (proof, title-deed; rendering Greek elegchos, Hebrew sepher)
etymology: From Latin evidentia, clearness. In Hebrew usage an evidence is a legal document — the deed itself, not an impression of one.
biblical_def: Evidence is proof, and in Scripture often the very deed of purchase. Hebrews defines faith with it: “faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb 11:1) — not a leap in the dark but the title-deed to what is real and not yet visible. Jeremiah acts it out at the worst possible moment, buying a field in a doomed country and signing the evidence: “I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it, and took witnesses” (Jer 32:10), because God had said houses and fields shall be possessed again in this land. Faith buys land in a besieged city.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines evidence as that which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; proof arising from our own perception or from the testimony of others.
webster_full: EVIDENCE, n. That which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; proof arising from our own perceptions by the senses, or from the testimony of others.
2. Any instrument or writing which contains proof.
3. A witness; one who testifies.
scriptures: Heb 11:1
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
And I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it, and took witnesses, and weighed him the money in the balances.
For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.
Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
corruption_summary: Faith is popularly defined as believing without evidence — the exact inversion of Hebrews 11:1, which calls faith the evidence itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The skeptic and the sentimental believer make the same mistake from opposite sides: both assume faith operates where proof is absent. Hebrews says faith is the evidence — the God-given assurance that functions as legal title to unseen realities. That is why biblical faith is never asked to float free of history. It rests on a resurrection with witnesses, a tomb that was inspected, and a Christ who invited Thomas to put his finger in the print of the nails.

Jeremiah 32 is the practical shape of it. The Babylonians were building siege works when God told him to buy his cousin's field, weigh the silver, sign and seal the evidence, and store the deed in an earthen vessel that it may continue many days. He purchased real property he could not visit, in a nation about to fall, because a promise had been given about what would come after. Every believer holding an unseen inheritance is doing the same paperwork.
roots_summary: Greek elegchos (G1650), proof, conviction, that which tests and demonstrates; Hebrew sepher (H5612), a written document, the deed of Jeremiah 32.
roots_lines: Greek elegchos (G1650) — proof, conviction; Hebrews 11:1, and 2 Timothy 3:16 of scripture profitable for reproof.
Hebrew sepher (H5612) — book, writing, deed; the evidence Jeremiah subscribed and sealed.
Greek hupostasis (G5287) — substance, confident assurance; the first half of Hebrews 11:1.
usage: “The evidence of things not seen” — faith as title-deed, not guesswork.
“I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it” — a purchase made in a doomed city.
“Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed” — sight is not the only proof.

pos: adj. (pure, undefiled; rendering Greek hagnos)
etymology: From Latin castus, pure, morally clean. The word covers more than sexual continence: it names an undivided loyalty.
biblical_def: Chaste means pure and undivided. Paul applies it to a whole congregation, not to individuals only: “I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2Co 11:2), and his fear in the next breath is doctrinal seduction — lest their minds be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. Peter directs it at the home, where a husband may be won “while they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear” (1Pe 3:2). Titus lists it among what older women are to teach the younger (Tit 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chaste as pure from all unlawful commerce of sexes; free from obscenity; and in language, pure and genuine, uncorrupt.
webster_full: CHASTE, a. Pure from all unlawful commerce of sexes. Applied to persons before marriage, it signifies pure from all sexual commerce, undefiled; after marriage, faithful to the marriage bed.
2. Free from obscenity.
3. In language, pure; genuine; uncorrupt; free from barbarous words and phrases.
scriptures: For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
While they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear.
Tit 2:5
To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed.
Jas 4:4
Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God.
corruption_summary: Chastity is treated as a rule about bodies imposed on the young, when Scripture treats it as covenant fidelity — which is why James calls idolatry adultery.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's use is the corrective the word needs. He is not warning the Corinthians about immorality in 2 Corinthians 11; he is warning them about another gospel, and he calls the danger unchastity. Doctrinal drift is marital infidelity because the church is betrothed. That single move explains why Scripture's prophets speak of idolatry in the language of whoredom and why James can write, ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God?

The domestic application in 1 Peter 3 is worth preserving against both a legalism that reduces it to hemlines and a permissiveness that empties it entirely. Peter's expectation is evangelistic: a husband who obeys not the word may be won without the word by the conversation of the wives. Chastity there is not merely restraint; it is a visible, attractive fidelity that argues for Christ without a syllable of argument.
roots_summary: Greek hagnos (G53), pure, sacredly clean — cognate with hagios, holy; the same word describes the wisdom from above as first pure.
roots_lines: Greek hagnos (G53) — pure, chaste; 2 Corinthians 11:2, 1 Peter 3:2, James 3:17, the wisdom that is from above is first pure.
Greek hagneia (G47) — purity; 1 Timothy 4:12, be thou an example in purity.
Greek parthenos (G3933) — virgin; the figure Paul uses of the whole church.
usage: “That I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” — the church betrothed, doctrine as fidelity.
“Your chaste conversation coupled with fear” — a life that argues without arguing.
“The friendship of the world is enmity with God” — worldliness named as adultery.

pos: adj. (disposed to peace; rendering Greek eirenikos)
etymology: From peace, Latin pax. Peaceable names a disposition rather than a circumstance — a man may be peaceable in a war.
biblical_def: Peaceable describes a settled disposition toward peace. James ranks it second in the wisdom from above: “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated” (Jas 3:17) — and the order is doctrine, since a peaceableness bought by surrendering purity is not this wisdom at all. Paul makes it the aim of prayer for rulers, “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2), and Hebrews promises that chastening yields “the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby” (Heb 12:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines peaceable as free from war, tumult or disorder; quiet; disposed to peace; not quarrelsome or turbulent.
webster_full: PEACEABLE, a. Free from war, tumult or public commotion.
2. Quiet; undisturbed; not agitated with passion.
3. Not quarrelsome; not turbulent; disposed to peace.
scriptures: Jas 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
corruption_summary: Peaceableness is confused with agreeableness — conflict avoidance rebranded as a fruit of the Spirit — and James's ordering, first pure then peaceable, is reversed.
corruption_paragraphs: James's sequence is the whole doctrine in two words. Purity comes first; peaceableness follows. A church that reverses the order will keep the peace by declining to name sin, and will call the silence love, but it has bought quiet with the very thing that made the wisdom heavenly. A church that keeps the order will sometimes be at war with error while remaining, in temperament, entirely peaceable — which is precisely what Christ was.

Paul's qualification in Romans 12:18 is honest about the limits: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. The two clauses concede that peace is not always possible and that another man's hostility is not always in our power to end. What is in our power is that the breach never originate with us — and Hebrews adds that the discipline of the Father produces this fruit in the trained, not in the merely comfortable.
roots_summary: Greek eirenikos (G1516), peaceable, from eirene (G1515), peace — the Septuagint's word for Hebrew shalom, wholeness.
roots_lines: Greek eirenikos (G1516) — peaceable; James 3:17 and Hebrews 12:11.
Greek eirenopoios (G1518) — peacemaker; Matthew 5:9, blessed are the peacemakers.
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, wholeness, welfare; far more than the absence of conflict.
usage: “First pure, then peaceable” — the order is the doctrine.
“A quiet and peaceable life in all godliness” — what to pray for rulers.
“If it be possible… live peaceably with all men” — honest about the limits.

pos: adj. (greedy of gain; rendering Greek pleonektes)
etymology: From Latin cupidus, desirous. The Greek pleonektes is literally one who wants more — the appetite defined by its lack of a stopping point.
biblical_def: Covetous describes the man who must have more. Scripture treats it as gravely as the sins that shock, listing the covetous among those who shall not inherit the kingdom (1Co 6:10), and Paul names it outright: “covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5). It is a disqualifier for church office — a bishop must be “not greedy of filthy lucre” (1Ti 3:3) — and Christ's warning gives the reason it is so hard to see: “Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines covetous as inordinately desirous, excessively eager to obtain and possess; directed to money or goods, avaricious.
webster_full: COVETOUS, a. Very desirous; eager to obtain; in a good sense, as covetous of wisdom.
2. Inordinately desirous; excessively eager to obtain and possess; directed to money or goods, avaricious.
scriptures: Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.
Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
corruption_summary: Covetousness is the one sin an entire economy is built to provoke, so the church has quietly reclassified it as ambition, aspiration, and good stewardship of opportunity.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's equation — covetousness, which is idolatry — explains why the tenth commandment reaches into the heart where no court can follow. Every other commandment can be kept outwardly by a man who wants to break it; covetousness is the wanting itself, and so it exposes what a man actually worships. That is also why it hides so well: no one confesses to idolatry while calling it a five-year plan.

Christ's antidote in Luke 12 is a redefinition of life rather than a rule about money. A man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth — and the parable that follows kills a man on the night his barns are finished. The rich fool is not condemned for farming well but for a soliloquy in which every pronoun is his own: my fruits, my barns, my goods, my soul. Covetousness is finally a grammar problem about ownership.
roots_summary: Greek pleonektes (G4123), one who wants more; philarguria (G5365), love of money; Hebrew batsa (H1215), unjust gain.
roots_lines: Greek pleonektes (G4123) — covetous, grasping; 1 Corinthians 5:11, 6:10, Ephesians 5:5.
Greek philarguria (G5365) — love of money; 1 Timothy 6:10, the root of all evil.
Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to desire, covet; the verb of the tenth commandment.
usage: “Covetousness, which is idolatry” — the sin that reveals the real god.
“A man's life consisteth not in the abundance” — a redefinition, not a budget rule.
“Not greedy of filthy lucre” — a standing disqualifier for office.

pos: n. (one who misleads; rendering Greek planos)
etymology: From Latin decipere, to ensnare. The Greek planos means a wanderer, and then one who makes others wander — a deceiver is a guide leading off the road.
biblical_def: A deceiver is one who leads others astray. John gives the New Testament's definition and its test in one verse: “many deceivers are entered into the world, who confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh. This is a deceiver and an antichrist” (2Jn 7). The mark is doctrinal — specifically Christological. Jacob is called a deceiver by his own father's trembling account (Gen 27:35 uses subtilty), Paul is slandered as one while being true — “as deceivers, and yet true” (2Co 6:8) — and the last deception is Satan's own, loosed to deceive the nations (Rev 20:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a deceiver as one who deceives; one who leads into error; a cheat; an impostor.
webster_full: DECEIVER, n. One who deceives; one who leads into error; a cheat; an impostor.
scriptures: 2Jn 7
For many deceivers are entered into the world, who confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh. This is a deceiver and an antichrist.
By honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report: as deceivers, and yet true;
Rev 20:8
And shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four quarters of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them together to battle: the number of whom is as the sand of the sea.
But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.
corruption_summary: Deception is now diagnosed by tone rather than doctrine — the harsh are suspected and the warm are trusted — when John's test is entirely about what a man says of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: John's criterion is uncomfortably narrow and therefore useful: does he confess that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh? Not, is he kind; not, is he effective; not, does he move a crowd. A deceiver in the apostolic sense may be gracious, generous, and personally admirable, and is far more dangerous for it. Conversely a blunt man who confesses Christ rightly is no deceiver, however much he grates.

2 Timothy 3:13 adds a detail that keeps the doctrine from becoming smug: evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived. The deceiver is himself deceived. This is not a class of cynical frauds who know better but a wandering that spreads, which is why Paul's remedy in the next verse is not exposure of others but continuance in what one has learned and been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned it.
roots_summary: Greek planos (G4108), wandering, a deceiver; planao (G4105), to cause to wander; the same root gives us planet, the wandering star.
roots_lines: Greek planos (G4108) — deceiver, impostor; 2 John 7, 1 Timothy 4:1 of seducing spirits.
Greek planao (G4105) — to lead astray; Matthew 24:4, take heed that no man deceive you.
Greek apate (G539) — deceitfulness; the deceitfulness of riches, Matthew 13:22.
usage: “Many deceivers are entered into the world” — the test is what he says of Christ.
“As deceivers, and yet true” — the faithful are sometimes so accused.
“Deceiving, and being deceived” — the deceiver is himself lost.

pos: adj. (obstinate; rendering Hebrew qesheh oreph, hard of neck)
etymology: A farming image: the ox that will not turn its neck to the yoke or the ploughman's rein. Scripture applies it to a nation that will not be led.
biblical_def: Stiffnecked means unwilling to be turned. It is God's own verdict at Sinai: “I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people” (Exo 32:9), spoken while the golden calf was still standing. The charge follows Israel through the wilderness — “circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked” (Deu 10:16) — and Stephen ends his sermon with it, which cost him his life: “Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost” (Act 7:51).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stiffnecked as stubborn, inflexibly obstinate, contumacious — citing the scriptural usage.
webster_full: STIFFNECKED, a. Stubborn; inflexibly obstinate; contumacious; as a stiffnecked people. Ex. 32.
scriptures: Exo 32:9
And the LORD said unto Moses, I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people:
Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked.
Act 7:51
Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.

Now be ye not stiffnecked, as your fathers were, but yield yourselves unto the LORD, and enter into his sanctuary, which he hath sanctified for ever: and serve the LORD your God, that the fierceness of his wrath may turn away from you. be
corruption_summary: Stubbornness is now marketed as conviction and authenticity — never back down, stay true to yourself — which is the exact temperament Scripture names as resisting the Holy Ghost.
corruption_paragraphs: The image is agricultural and unflattering. A stiff-necked animal is not brave; it is useless, unable to be guided and therefore unable to work. When God calls Israel stiffnecked He is not describing spirited independence but a beast that will not take direction, and the remedy He prescribes is surgical rather than motivational: circumcise the foreskin of your heart. Obstinacy is not fixed by resolve; it is fixed by a new heart.

Stephen's application is the one the church needs, because he aimed it at the most religious men in Jerusalem. Ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye. Stiffneckedness is perfectly compatible with orthodoxy, temple attendance, and scriptural literacy — it merely requires that a man decide in advance which corrections he will not receive. That is why the sermon ended in stones.
roots_summary: Hebrew qesheh (H7186), hard, severe, with oreph (H6203), the back of the neck — literally hard of neck; Greek sklerotrachelos (G4644) in Acts 7:51.
roots_lines: Hebrew qesheh oreph (H7186/H6203) — hard of neck; Exodus 32:9, 33:3, Deuteronomy 9:6.
Greek sklerotrachelos (G4644) — stiffnecked; only Acts 7:51, Stephen's charge.
Hebrew arel (H6189) — uncircumcised; paired with stiffnecked in Deuteronomy 10:16 and Acts 7:51.
usage: “Behold, it is a stiffnecked people” — the verdict spoken over the golden calf.
“Circumcise… your heart, and be no more stiffnecked” — the remedy is surgical.
“Ye do always resist the Holy Ghost” — orthodoxy is no protection.
